questions.q: State the formula used to calculate the central angle of a sector in a pie diagram when the data are given as percentages.
questions.a: The formula is: Angle = Percentage × 3.6 (since 360°/100 = 3.6). A wrong answer such as "Angle = Percentage × 360" reveals the student has forgotten to divide by 100, leading to angles 100 times too large and an impossible diagram.

questions.q: Why does the NCERT textbook recommend arranging the angles in ascending order and plotting them clockwise starting with the smallest angle?
questions.a: Starting with the smallest angle minimises the accumulation of measurement errors; if you begin with a large angle, any small protractor error gets magnified for the remaining tiny sectors, making them hard to plot accurately. A student who says "it looks better" misses the precision rationale and would likely produce diagrams with overlapping or gapped sectors.

questions.q: Given the following data on India's land use (1950-51): Net Sown Area 42%, Forest 14%, Not available for cultivation 17%, Fallow Land 10%, Pasture and Tree 9%, Culturable Waste Land 8%. Calculate the central angle for each category and verify that the sum of angles equals 360°.
questions.a:
Step 1: Multiply each percentage by 3.6.  
Net Sown Area: 42 × 3.6 = 151.2°  
Forest: 14 × 3.6 = 50.4°  
Not available: 17 × 3.6 = 61.2°  
Fallow Land: 10 × 3.6 = 36.0°  
Pasture and Tree: 9 × 3.6 = 32.4°  
Culturable Waste: 8 × 3.6 = 28.8°  
Step 2: Sum = 151.2 + 50.4 + 61.2 + 36.0 + 32.4 + 28.8 = 360.0°.  
A wrong sum (e.g., 359.8° or 360.5°) indicates rounding errors or a miscalculation in one category; the student should re-check each multiplication.

questions.q: A student draws a pie diagram for the same land-use data but starts plotting with the largest angle (151.2°) and proceeds clockwise. The final sector (Culturable Waste, 28.8°) does not close the circle perfectly; a gap of 2° remains. Explain why this happened and how the ascending-order rule prevents it.
questions.a: When the largest angle is plotted first, any small protractor error (say +0.5°) is repeated for each subsequent sector. By the time the last small sector is drawn, the cumulative error may exceed the sector's own angle, leaving a gap or overlap. Ascending order confines the cumulative error to the largest sector at the end, where a 2° discrepancy is visually negligible. A student who blames "poor protractor quality" misses the systematic error-propagation concept.

questions.q: Evaluate the suitability of a pie diagram for representing the following dataset: "Monthly rainfall (cm) in Delhi for 12 months". Justify your answer with two reasons.
questions.a: A pie diagram is unsuitable because: (1) Rainfall data is a time series; a line/bar graph shows temporal trends better. (2) The total of monthly rainfall is not a meaningful "whole" — the sum of monthly rainfalls does not represent a fixed total like 100% of exports. A student who says "pie diagrams can show any data" fails to recognise that pie diagrams require parts of a meaningful whole.

questions.q: Design a pie diagram to represent the percentage distribution of India's population by religion (hypothetical data: Hindu 79.8%, Muslim 14.2%, Christian 2.3%, Sikh 1.7%, Buddhist 0.7%, Jain 0.4%, Others 0.9%). Specify the radius, the order of sectors, the shading pattern, and the legend format you would use for a board-exam answer sheet.
questions.a: Radius: 4 cm (fits A4 sheet). Angles: Hindu 287°, Muslim 51°, Christian 8°, Sikh 6°, Buddhist 2.5°, Jain 1.4°, Others 3.2° (rounded). Order ascending: Jain (1.4°), Buddhist (2.5°), Others (3.2°), Christian (8°), Sikh (6°), Muslim (51°), Hindu (287°). Wait — ascending order means Jain (1.4°), Buddhist (2.5°), Others (3.2°), Christian (8°), Sikh (6°)? Actually 6° < 8°, so Sikh before Christian. Correct ascending: Jain (1.4°), Buddhist (2.5°), Others (3.2°), Sikh (6°), Christian (8°), Muslim (51°), Hindu (287°). Shading: distinct patterns (horizontal, vertical, diagonal, dots, cross-hatch, solid, blank). Legend: bottom-right, each pattern with religion name and percentage. A poor answer would omit the ascending order, use radius 10 cm (too large), or forget the legend.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A pie diagram (or divided circle diagram) is a two-dimensional graphical ______ where a circle is divided into sectors whose central angles are proportional to the magnitudes of the data categories they represent, such that the entire circle corresponds to the total value (100% or the sum of all values) and each sector's angle = (category value / total value) × 360°.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are looking at the "Direction of Indian ______ 2010–11" in a newspaper: a colourful circle split into slices labelled Europe 20%, Asia 56%, etc.
Fill in the blank: Take the export percentages, multiply each by ______ to get the angle, then arrange the angles from smallest to largest.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently construct a pie diagram from raw data: calculate percentages, derive sector angles using the 3.6 multiplier, draw the circle with an appropriate radius, plot sectors in ascending order of angle clockwise using a protractor, and add a complete legend with distinct shading.
